content.title: The government, households, property and the economic cycle
content.description: The election is approaching. Recently, the government has devoted considerable resources to strengthening households’ purchasing power through measures such as a new earned income tax credit, lower VAT on food and lower electricity tax. The housing market is being stimulated through measures including higher borrowing limits, exemption from mortgage repayment requirements and a building permit reform.
content.extendedDescription: Is this enough to revive households’ appetite for spending and the sluggish housing market? The government is pursuing a housing policy that, among other things, speeds up chains of home moves, facilitates new construction and helps young people into their first home. Could further stimulus measures be considered? Could freer rent-setting resolve some of the difficulties?
speakerTitles: State Secretary to the Minister for Housing

content.title: Echoing emptiness: the market and new challenges
content.description: Vacancy rates in several property segments are higher than they have been for a long time: rental housing, offices, shops and logistics. This naturally holds the market back and may put downward pressure on rents. What is the situation in the different segments now? What is the trend – is a turnaround in sight?
content.extendedDescription:
What is happening to vacancies, rents and values? Does Sweden differ from international trends?
Changes in society, technology, the pandemic and the economy have had a major impact on commercial property in recent years. Demographic changes also have an impact. There is widespread scepticism about offices. Do companies and public authorities need so much office space? Can we use our existing buildings more efficiently? Will demand return? Have we built homes in the wrong places again, or are homes becoming vacant in areas with shrinking populations?

content.title: Does increased security in schools create greater reassurance or greater anxiety?
content.description: A safe school is a prerequisite for learning. Today we talk a lot about security in schools, but can the mere feeling that school is a dangerous place create a sense of insecurity? Is a school’s role to educate – or to police? And does safety lie in detailed measures or in the collective capability of the staff?
content.extendedDescription:
We will discuss the following questions:
•	How is the sense of safety among staff and school leaders affected by the message that Swedish schools are dangerous places?
•	Can an excessive focus on security create a perceived lack of safety?
•	What do we know – what data is available on crime and incidents in school environments?
•	Knowledge tailored to the target audience: do staff feel safer or more frightened after training?
•	The balance between detailed planning and generally improved capability?
•	The role of schools: policing or education?
content.subject: Education

content.title: Few women at the top: how do we break the glass ceiling to CEO and chair roles?
content.description: Business is becoming more gender-equal, but the number of women serving as CEOs and chairs of the largest companies remains small. Why is this, and what is needed to increase gender equality in the highest positions in business?
content.extendedDescription:
We discuss:
What are the biggest barriers to women reaching CEO and chair roles – are they about structures, culture or something else?
How do informal networks and recruitment processes affect women’s opportunities to reach the top?
What role do role models and mentors play in helping more women reach the top?
Are there differences between industries in women’s opportunities to reach leadership positions – and what can other industries learn from those that have been more successful?
How can companies and boards work in more concrete, results-oriented ways to break the glass ceiling?
What responsibility do men in leadership positions have for driving gender equality efforts?
speakerTitles: Minister for Gender Equality and Working Life

content.title: Quest for Talent: The Game Industry’s Commitments to Diversity, Inclusion, Equality and Education
content.description: Talent supply is one of the critical challenges of the future. How can we open doors for new talent, broaden the recruitment base, and secure skills for the games industry, and for society as a whole?
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar highlights four initiatives shaping the future talent of the games industry.

Futuregames & Tencent Partnership: Supporting the next generation of game devs in Sweden and Poland. Tencent provides mentorship, aiming to equip students with the skills needed and strengthen the talent pipeline.

King & SGI Scholarship: Introduces women, trans and non-binary individuals to the games industry through mentorship and networking, addressing gender imbalance by creating new pathways.

Video Games Europe working with UNICEF Game Changers Coalition: A global forum uniting companies, governments, and young leaders to close the gender digital gap by promoting STEAM skills for girls worldwide.

Games for Change Learn program: Invites students to create games inspired by the UN Sustainable Development Goals, combining STEAM skills with social impact. Educators receive training to integrate game design into curricula, fostering creativity and problem-solving.

content.title: Democracy Defence Level Up: Threats to democracy in gaming environments?
content.description: At a time when disinformation and fake news spread rapidly and democratic principles are being challenged, we need to strengthen society’s ability to resist manipulation. Can games provide a platform for raising awareness, building resilience and promoting critical thinking?
content.extendedDescription:
Threats to democracy in gaming environments?
Are there threats to democracy in gaming environments, and if so, what do they look like? Democratic debate should be characterised by openness and the ability to take a position without facing threats and hate, but what is the situation in our gaming environments? What risks of influence and anti-democratic activity do players see?

content.title: University healthcare: Sweden’s window to the world for clinical research
content.description: Sweden is losing ground in clinical studies. Fewer studies are conducted here, and our attractiveness is declining. But we cannot, and should not, compete on size. We should compete on quality, specialist expertise and collaboration. We also have unique opportunities for registry-based clinical trials.
content.extendedDescription:
Through our university hospitals and strong life science environments, Sweden has a unique opportunity to offer something more: advanced and academic studies, innovative substudies and a high degree of delivery reliability. When university hospitals collaborate regionally and nationally, they create a larger shared pool of potential participants, faster implementation and clear international competitiveness.

Swedish University Hospital Alliance (SUHA) brings together all of Sweden’s university hospitals and provides the platform for strengthening Sweden’s position in clinical research.

In this seminar, SUHA and Uppsala universitet highlight how national coordination can free up resources and strengthen quality – so that every research effort delivers the greatest possible benefit for patients, healthcare and society.

content.title: Moral panic and screen policy: the political youth organisations have their say
content.description: Screen time, age limits and video gaming – where is the line between justified concern and excessive panic? How can society and policymakers address the realities of young people’s digital lives without falling into the classic trap of moral panic?
content.extendedDescription:
First came the imaginary worlds of books, then the unnatural speed of trains, followed by jazz, video violence and now: screen time. In an age of panic about protecting children from evil, we discuss everything from limiting screen time to shutting young people out of certain digital worlds altogether. What is a timer on screen use worth, and what actually happens behind the screen? A digital culture is emerging in which games, platforms and social media can be places for entertainment, cultural creation, socialising and learning, while also presenting risks and threats to avoid.

This is not the first time youth culture has come under society’s scrutiny, which is why SpelAlmedalen is inviting political youth organisations to an open dialogue. How do young people’s digital lives affect political debate, and how does political debate affect young people’s digital lives? And do young people themselves think that adults in power are proposing the right methods to “solve the problem”?

content.title: The trends shaping the future of collective mobility: how are metropolitan regions preparing?
content.description: Collective mobility is expected to face major changes ahead. Robotaxis are just around the corner, the sustainability argument for travelling collectively has weakened, and public transport must serve both urban groups with high expectations of comfort and rural residents facing different circumstances. How can this be reconciled?
content.extendedDescription:
We look to the future and explore trends in collective mobility. Our starting point is a report from K2 that identifies several scenarios. How will people want to travel in the future? Which innovations and societal factors are driving developments? What happens when new global technology companies meet traditional Swedish public transport administration? How can new mobility services and shared vehicles become part of the transport system of the future, and how can public transport authorities respond to its many new and varied needs?

The panel will discuss current societal trends and what they mean for future travel, focusing on how public transport and other shared mobility solutions can become more attractive choices for more people.

You are welcome to listen and contribute to the discussion.

content.title: Does youth involvement in associations work in outer-city areas?
content.description: Young people’s engagement is declining in Sweden, despite reports showing that young people want to get involved. We see a gap between formal and informal engagement – what makes it less daunting to organise things outside an association? Is the association model in its current form outdated?
content.extendedDescription:
A discussion with young people about youth engagement in outer-city areas.

The gaming culture and youth organisation Sverok runs the Trygga Spelplatser project, which works to reach young people who experience racism in outer-city areas across Sweden and create a more inclusive gaming culture. Part of this work involves supporting young people in starting associations or joining Sverok associations. Our experiences from this work have prompted us to invite more civil society organisations working to engage young people in outer-city areas, along with young people active in associations, to a broader conversation to discuss and learn from one another.

We see a gap between formal and informal engagement – what makes it less daunting to organise things outside an association? Is the association model in its current form outdated? If it does not help young people meet, create and organise – who is the association model for?

content.title: Games save lives
content.description: Games are now an important social and cultural space for many people. How can games strengthen people’s capacity to live and be used to create safe, inclusive environments and develop important skills? How can decision-makers support gaming culture as an important part of everyday life for young people and adults?
content.extendedDescription:
Games can strengthen mental health and social connections and provide a vital space for young people. How can we use these insights?
A seminar in 4 parts:

Research shows that playfulness helps us learn, collaborate and adapt to change. Uppsala universitet is investigating how playable systems can promote health and learning, as well as the ability to live, participate and contribute on one’s own terms.

The report “Power of Play 2025” shows that gaming promotes mental health, social interaction, creativity and critical thinking. A global study involving more than 24000 players.

The report “Mer än ett spel” focuses on young people with neurodevelopmental conditions (NPF). It shows that gaming culture is a space for social interaction, personal development and recovery. Games provide a vital space where young people with NPF can feel included and understood.

From exclusion to hope for the future – FCV Sverige engages young people furthest from education through game-based courses that strengthen motivation and self-confidence. 98% go on to further studies or work.

content.title: Future-proofing elder care through innovative and preventive measures
content.description: More and more people are living longer – but more years also mean greater needs for support and care. For elder care to be sustainable, the focus must shift from responding to needs late to working preventively, improving older people’s health and creating more healthy years.
content.extendedDescription:
What practical steps can municipalities take to respond to demographic change while strengthening older people’s health and independence? During the seminar, you will hear practical examples of preventive and health-promoting measures that can help delay the need for more extensive care.
We present approaches and measures already being tested in Swedish municipalities and discuss the results they can deliver – both for older people and for municipalities’ long-term sustainability. You will also hear about the organisational changes needed to shift successfully from a reactive to a more preventive approach.
The seminar also shows how this type of initiative can be financed through a social outcomes contract. In this model, an external investor initially funds the measures, and the municipality repays only if and as agreed outcomes are achieved. This enables municipalities to undertake important preventive initiatives without bearing the entire financial risk from the outset.
speakerTitles: Head of Preventive Measures for Older People
Chair of the Municipal Executive Board
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: How, and with which methods, can we help young people leave crime and enter employment?
content.description: Youth crime is causing great concern, while many young people lack routes out of criminal environments. Reversing this trend requires approaches that combine support, relationships and practical pathways into employment.
content.extendedDescription:
How can more young people leave crime behind and move into employment and independent lives? The seminar presents the approach behind Trygg Rätt – a model combining relationship-based support with clear pathways into employment and earning a living.
The starting point is to work with entire groups of young people from the same area and create a setting where participants receive support to break away from destructive environments, build new relationships and establish themselves in the labour market. The results are remarkable: 80% of participants go on to work or study.
During the seminar, you will hear how the model is structured, which components are crucial to success and what has been learned in practice.
A financing model is also presented in which a social outcomes contract makes the initiative possible. This means that an external investor funds the intervention in advance, and public-sector organisations pay only if and as agreed outcomes are achieved.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: How can practical understanding of sustainable materials expand circular construction?
content.description: The construction sector faces major challenges and needs to change. We need to introduce circular construction in which we care for what is already built and learn to use reclaimed products combined with new building materials that have a low impact on the climate and environment.
content.extendedDescription: There are already successful examples of circular construction at scale. We have created a workshop space where everyone interested is welcome to get to know reclaimed brick products and unfired clay mortars and plasters, and learn how to build on what already exists. This is a hands-on materials tent where you can physically explore new sustainable building materials and understand how they can be used at scale. Try laying Swedish CE-marked reclaimed bricks with clay mortar, or plastering a beautiful wall with different clay plasters. Or why not visit the neighbouring Cirkulära Mötesplatsen and try Sgraffito, scratching your message into clay while discussing sustainable construction? Here you will meet both invited key figures from the construction industry and curious visitors who stop by to talk about circular construction in practice!
content.subject: Sustainability
content.accessibility: Wheelchair-accessible entrance and venue
content.detail: Circular building materials tent & meeting place

content.description: The construction sector faces major challenges and needs to change. We need to introduce circular construction in which we care for what is already built and learn to use reclaimed products combined with new building materials that have a low impact on the climate and environment.
content.extendedDescription: There are already successful examples of circular construction at scale. We have created a workshop space where everyone interested is welcome to get to know reclaimed brick products and unfired clay mortars and plasters, and learn how to build on what already exists. This is a hands-on materials tent where you can physically explore new sustainable building materials and understand how they can be used at scale. Try laying Swedish CE-marked reclaimed bricks with clay mortar, or plastering a beautiful wall with different clay plasters. Or why not visit the neighbouring Cirkulära Mötesplatsen and try Sgraffito, scratching your message into clay while discussing sustainable construction? content.title: Working together for robust supply preparedness: a hot potato
content.description: How can we strengthen Sweden’s supply preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
We live in increasingly insecure times. Geopolitical uncertainty, climate change and major societal transitions mean that municipalities, public authorities, businesses and civil society need to find simple forms of cooperation that work over the long term. Conditions vary between counties and municipalities, but all share the goal and responsibility of keeping residents safe. An important part is supply capacity and preparedness, which require critical resources such as electricity and food.

The government has presented a proposal for state stockpiling in the food supply chain. To strengthen resilience in crises and war, municipalities also need to build up emergency stocks quickly. But do current regulations allow the cooperation that is needed?

A light lunch will be served after the seminar.
content.subject: Innovation

Opening by the Commanding officer of the Gotland Regiment P18

The exhibition Through Their Eyes brings together two powerful projects — Chasiv Yar – Fireproof and the award-winning Frontline Rolls — revealing the reality of war through the eyes of Ukrainian soldiers.

Chasiv Yar – Fireproof is dedicated to the defense of Chasiv Yar by soldiers of the 24th Separate Mechanized Brigade named after King Danylo. The photographs are displayed on fragments of a fence from the Donetsk region, damaged by Russian shelling, as well as within the exhibition tent — grounding the images directly in the material reality of war.

Frontline Rolls — winner of the 2026 PHMuseum Prize — offers a deeply personal insight into the lives and inner worlds of soldiers on the front line. By sending disposable film cameras to different sections of the front line, project author Sergey Melnitchenko gave soldiers the opportunity to document their own reality. The result is a unique archive of wartime testimonies.

content.title: How can we create barriers to prevent catastrophic fires like the one in Crans-Montana?
content.description: In January 2026, a devastating fire broke out at a nightclub in the ski resort of Crans-Montana, Switzerland, killing more than 40 people and injuring more than 100. What allows serious fire disasters to happen, how can we prevent similar death traps in Sweden, and what responsibility do policymakers have?
content.extendedDescription:
Fires with catastrophic consequences occur repeatedly. It has been 28 years since the fire at Backaplan in Göteborg that claimed the lives of 63 young people. What are the underlying factors in serious fire disasters? What can we do to build resilience against catastrophic fires? Is new legislation needed, and could a new model for systematic fire safety management be part of the solution?

After the Grenfell Tower fire in London in 2017, which claimed 72 lives, the British government apologised for its lack of commitment to fire safety. Leadership commitment creates the conditions for a sound safety culture that can permeate society, from government to workplaces.

During the seminar, we present lessons from catastrophic fires and invite a prominent panel to discuss how to create robust fire protection.

content.title: Young people’s leisure time in crisis: from unwanted loneliness to happy gamer
content.description: More and more young people experience unwanted loneliness, while thriving associations await in gaming worlds. We highlight the role of gaming culture as a vital space for social connection and ask: how can we reverse the loneliness crisis by investing in young people’s interests?
content.extendedDescription:
Unwanted loneliness among young people is a growing social problem with serious consequences for mental health and society as a whole. At the same time, there is enormous potential in the digital and physical communities of gaming culture. For many young people, gaming is more than a hobby: it is a vital space for social interaction, with low barriers to entry and a welcoming environment. Yet there are also online threats and risks in the form of anti-democratic movements and radicalisation. How can we work towards safe and meaningful leisure time in a digital age?
Having meaningful leisure time is not only a right for young people; it is one of the most important protective factors against social exclusion. To resolve the crisis in young people’s leisure time, we must understand and support the environments where they themselves choose to build their communities.

content.title: A divided society – a divided democracy? The significance of segregation for political participation
content.description: What is the relationship between segregation and democratic participation?
content.extendedDescription:
We examine the relationship between segregation and democratic participation. In recent decades, segregation has increased in many parts of society, for example between residential areas, schools and workplaces. These differences mean that people increasingly live their everyday lives in different social environments, with different resources, experiences and networks.

At the same time, there are clear differences in political participation, such as voter turnout and other forms of political engagement, between groups and areas. We present research on how these differences have evolved over time and how they relate to different forms of segregation. content.title: AI in the games industry: toy, threat or opportunity?
content.description: AI affects every industry. But what is AI, really, and what could it do for the games industry? What challenges and opportunities does AI present for games, beyond generative content alone?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is an angel or a demon, depending on whom you ask. At one end: an environmental villain, a threat to creativity, a cause of unemployment and ethically questionable. At the other: a saviour and a force for disruptive transformation that could change the course of the whole world. Which picture is closest to the truth? For many, AI is synonymous with Gemini and ChatGPT, but how could it be used to strengthen protections for young players online, give small businesses more resources to develop good products, or improve the quality of game programming? And how do various initiatives fit into this, such as the European AI factories where supercomputers with different specialisations give small and medium-sized businesses access to enormous computing power free of charge?

RISE / Mimer AI Factory is providing breakfast!

content.title: Solar panels, batteries and timber buildings: can fire protection keep up with the energy transition?
content.description: The energy transition is a necessary change in society. The question is not whether to make the transition, but how to ensure robust fire protection at the same time. Fire safety is often considered too late, and short-term interests take precedence. How can we avoid building up a fire safety deficit that must be addressed later?
content.extendedDescription:
After several weak years, forecasts point to an increase in construction. This growth is linked to the green transition, as the industry shifts towards lower carbon emissions, greater circularity and energy efficiency through measures such as solar panels and battery storage. But how can we ensure that the transition does not come at the expense of lives and property?

The transition brings risks that current regulations and fire protection methods are not always equipped to address. We risk building in future fire safety problems. How can we meet requirements for circularity and bio-based materials without compromising fire safety? How can we manage the fire risks associated with large-scale battery storage and solar installations in densely built-up areas?

A discussion with representatives from the construction industry, academia and policymakers to find forms of collaboration in which sustainability and resilience go hand in hand.

content.title: Can we have total defence without an engaged civil society?
content.description: The government is investing 4.6 billion in local preparedness in 2026–2028 and establishing a civil defence agency. But a crucial question remains: how do we build long-term, funded integration of civil society organisations? How do we move from words to action when we say everyone should contribute?
content.extendedDescription:
From 700 to 75 000 civilian first responders – what does it take to mobilise all of society?
When an accident or crisis occurs, an ordinary person is often first on the scene. Through Civil insatsperson (CIP), that person receives training, equipment and a way to receive alerts – and can save lives before the emergency services arrive. Today there are around 700 CIP in Sweden and more than 2 900 waiting to join. Initiatives like this need to be an integral part of civic engagement and defence, yet the agency has only been given the ability to support a small proportion of civil society organisations.

The seminar will discuss:
How civil society can contribute
What is needed in governance and government appropriation directions
How the state, municipalities and businesses share responsibility
Whether voluntary initiatives should receive clear national funding

A discussion about safety, trust – and whether Sweden can rise to the challenge when it really matters.

SäkerhetsArenan: SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Tryggare Sverige, Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and SOFF.

content.title: Who takes responsibility for smaller companies’ cybersecurity?
content.description: Cyberattacks against companies in Sweden are a constant reality. Smaller companies are particularly vulnerable and can, for example, be exploited to gain access to supply chains. How can we strengthen their ability to prevent and limit the effects of a cyberattack?
content.extendedDescription:
Cyberattacks pose a real and constant threat to Sweden and our digitalised society. They cause not only economic damage but can also undermine trust in our institutions and companies. Small companies are particularly exposed because of limited cybersecurity capabilities. Their vulnerabilities are exploited, for example, in attacks on larger companies in the supply chain.

How can we develop smaller companies’ cybersecurity capabilities to both prevent and mitigate the effects of an attack? How can we reach them when, for example, only 17% train their own staff? Who takes responsibility for ensuring this happens?

Welcome to a discussion on strengthening smaller companies’ cybersecurity so that they also contribute to society’s overall cybersecurity capability.

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet, Säkerhets- och försvarsföretagen (SOFF).

content.title: The demographic challenge: where and how should older people live?
content.description: Sweden’s demographic trend is clear: we are living longer and having fewer children. By 2030, there will be more than 150 000 more people aged over 80 than today, bringing the total to over 800 000.
content.extendedDescription:
The growing older population presents a challenge for society as a whole, and especially for the housing sector, to provide more homes that offer greater dignity for older people. How do we want older people to live in the future? Should we convert preschools into care homes? Should we think more about multigenerational housing? Is new support for housing for older people needed? And what incentives are needed for older people to leave houses that are too large and not adapted to their needs, thereby making room for families with children?
Bostadspolitik.se, together with a number of industry representatives, is organising the go-to arena for housing policy in Almedalen – at Clarion Hotel Wisby (Paviljongen) on Tuesday and Wednesday.

content.title: Evidence in the DNA of everyday practice: Living and Policy Labs in municipal health and social care
content.description: Municipalities bear growing overall responsibility for both healthcare and social care – at the intersection of the Patient Act and the new Social Services Act. How do we build evidence and proven experience when systems, legal provisions and governance clash? How can shared ownership in partnerships enable small-scale testing and learning?
content.extendedDescription:
Municipal responsibilities span home healthcare, care and social services – where the Patient Act and the new Social Services Act meet everyday priorities, workforce needs and a wide range of governance systems. When legal provisions and approaches differ, knowledge risks becoming siloed: healthcare is professionally governed and more evidence-driven, while care and social services often have other bases for decisions. This contributes to variation and inequality, particularly in elder care, and creates clashes between organisations and responsibilities.
The seminar starts from the premise that evidence cannot be “delivered” by a single organisation: municipalities, regions, the state and academia need to take joint responsibility and share ownership of what should be tested, how it is measured and how lessons are put into practice. We discuss how partnerships and test environments – GPCC’s various Living & Policy Labs, OMTÄNKT and DEMSAM – can provide practical ways to test on a small scale without going all in, using shared structures for data and learning.

content.title: Hydrogen for a stronger Sweden
content.description: Hydrogen is an important part of the energy system of the future and the industrial transition, but it has also been questioned in public debate. Do we really need hydrogen – and if so, for what?
content.extendedDescription:
At Arena Vätgas 2026, we highlight why hydrogen is essential to future-proofing industry, the energy system and transport.
The seminar will discuss how hydrogen can benefit the energy system, security of supply, competitiveness and preparedness, and which barriers are currently slowing development. Despite technically mature projects and major industrial ambitions, demand remains limited, and in many cases business models are insufficiently developed to enable investment decisions.

Arena Vätgas will offer perspectives from industrial and energy companies with experience of concrete hydrogen projects and value chains, as well as from research, public authorities and politics, on how hydrogen can contribute to a stronger Sweden, locally and nationally.

Arena Vätgas is a shared meeting place for industry, the energy sector and politics to discuss how climate ambitions, competitiveness and a system-wide perspective can come together in practice.

content.title: The value of data to criminals and the rise of data cartels
content.description: Every day, we give away data when we use apps, shop or move through digital environments. This information drives innovation and development but can also be used against us. It raises questions about control, responsibility and risks to society and security.
content.extendedDescription:
Data is now collected on an unprecedented scale. When information is combined, analysed and refined, it can be used to influence decisions, steer behaviour and target crimes such as fraud, extortion, manipulation and sabotage. At the same time, control over data is becoming an increasingly important economic and strategic resource.

During the seminar, we explore how an increasingly data-driven economy can affect society, business and security. Drawing on analyses from the Framtidens brott report series, we discuss possible developments, from new forms of crime to the emergence of data cartels, and the choices that may become important in the future.

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet, Säkerhets- och försvarsföretagen (SOFF). content.description: Officials’ or politicians’ personal opinions often delay housing projects and make them more expensive.
content.extendedDescription:

content.title: Cybersecurity is high on the agenda, but how do we strengthen skills throughout Sweden?
content.description: Legislation is becoming stricter, technological development is accelerating and cyberattacks are increasing. At the same time, many organisations lack a systematic approach to cybersecurity and a structure for putting it into practice. How do we strengthen the skills of boards, management and employees?
content.extendedDescription:
How do we strengthen cybersecurity in Sweden when many organisations underestimate the risks and few invest in training?
Several surveys show that many organisations are not particularly concerned about cybercrime and that few train their staff in cybersecurity.
The Cybersecurity Act has now been in force for 5 months. What has happened since then?
The aim is to turn understanding into decisions and action, to protect organisations and strengthen society’s resilience. This must involve close collaboration between the public sector, business and academia.
There is a broader purpose: to equip Sweden with cybersecurity skills. This is where we stand, and we share a desire to raise the issue.
SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Almega Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet

content.title: Three months with the new mortgage rules
content.description: New mortgage rules were introduced on 1 April. The loan-to-value cap was raised to 90 per cent, the most recent amortisation requirement was removed, a new cap on additional borrowing was introduced (at 80 per cent of the property’s value), and revaluations are generally only permitted every five years.
content.extendedDescription:
The new mortgage rules have been debated for several years, and the debate has continued since their introduction. Supporters argue that the new rules help first-time buyers enter the home ownership market, while others argue that they drive up prices, making it harder to enter the market anyway. There are also concerns about increased indebtedness. The restrictions on additional borrowing have met with sharp criticism: critics argue that they make renovations harder to finance and create difficulties in the event of separation and for various shared-ownership models. By the time this seminar takes place, the new rules will have been in use for almost three months. We discuss the initial impressions – have the fears been borne out?

content.title: The role of single-family homes in meeting future housing needs
content.description: Single-family homes remain the type of housing most sought after by households, particularly families with children and people starting families. At the same time, construction of new single-family homes is at a historic low. The challenges are particularly evident outside major cities, where construction costs have risen much more than willingness to pay and property values.
content.extendedDescription:
It often costs more to build a home than the completed property can be sold for. This makes single-family housing projects difficult to deliver, even in municipalities with growing populations, housing shortages and political ambitions to grow.
Credit restrictions and uncertain financing limit households’ purchasing power. For developers, this means increased risks, higher capital requirements and projects that fail banks’ risk and profitability assessments. For municipalities, it makes housing provision targets difficult to meet. The consequences include reduced mobility in the housing market, greater difficulties in starting a family, weaker growth and increased pressure on rental and tenant-owned housing, even where single-family homes are actually the most sought-after and practical form of housing. This session analyses and discusses the situation and the challenges.

content.title: With God in politics – is Christian nationalism a threat to democracy?

content.title: Who will win the battle for the next generation of digital talent – gangs or society?
content.description: The recruitment of children for everything from cybercrime to acts of violence has increasingly moved to digital meeting places, where technological development often outpaces legislation. This takes place on platforms and in gaming environments used by large numbers of young people. What can be done to reverse the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
The recruitment of children for everything from cybercrime to acts of violence has increasingly moved from SiS institutions, HVB residential care homes and sports settings to digital meeting places, where technological development often outpaces legislation. This takes place on platforms and in gaming environments used by large numbers of young people, such as TikTok, Roblox and Fortnite.

In a unique collaboration between Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige, Polismyndigheten, Swedbank and around 20 municipalities, we show how a public–private partnership creates real alternatives for young people in digital risk environments. The HackShield concept strengthens children’s and young people’s resilience to everything from online fraud and money laundering to online hate, disinformation and recruitment attempts. At the same time, the collaboration encourages children’s interest in digital technology, which can create future career opportunities.

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Tryggare Sverige, Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and SOFF.

content.title: Welcome, and go home – what do young people say about democracy, discrimination and their chance to make a difference?
content.description: How are young people affected by discrimination, racism and new laws? Why is young people’s participation in democracy declining, and why are they so rarely allowed to help shape the solutions? What are young people’s perspectives and ideas about what needs to change to create a more inclusive and democratic society?
content.extendedDescription: When can I be sure whether I will be allowed to stay in Sweden? How many generations does it take to be considered Swedish? Why are some young people labelled as problems or criminals? Why is there so little discussion of racism and discrimination when they have become an everyday experience for some young people? What consequences are we seeing from the many new laws and reforms? Voter turnout among young people in areas affected by social exclusion has fallen by 10%. Why are no initiatives being launched to support democracy and the election? And why do we not include the people we so often talk ABOUT IN THE CONVERSATIONS and in the solutions? If young people could decide, what would we invest in and what would we scrap? And how do we work to influence change today?
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Sweden’s new security landscape – which threats are shaping the society of the future?
content.description: Sweden’s security environment is changing rapidly. Cyberattacks, information influence operations, insider threats and vulnerable supply chains affect both the public sector and business. What does the new threat landscape look like, and which risks might we underestimate in an increasingly complex security landscape?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden’s security challenges have changed fundamentally in recent years. Threats previously regarded as technical or specific to individual sectors now affect society as a whole. Cyberattacks, information influence operations, insider issues and vulnerable dependencies in supply chains can have major consequences for both essential services and the private sector.

This seminar discusses how the security landscape is evolving and the implications for organisations and decision-makers. Which threats will be most critical to Sweden’s security in the coming years? How does the risk landscape change when technology, geopolitics and societal dependencies become intertwined? And how can organisations better understand and respond to a more complex security environment? The event takes the form of a moderated discussion bringing together different perspectives on future security challenges.

content.title: Is the monarchy more expensive than you think?
content.description: In the debate about the form of government, it is sometimes claimed that the monarchy is inexpensive. Our scrutiny of the royal household shows that the actual cost of the Swedish monarchy is far higher than it is often portrayed.
content.extendedDescription:
Republikanska föreningen presents a new report on the true costs of the monarchy. Funding of the royal household is very difficult to scrutinise because not everything that should be counted is included in any official compilation, and because inaccurate claims are spread by the royal court. Republikanska föreningen is not seeking the cheapest form of government, but we do want the most democratic one. However, the amount of taxpayers’ money going to the monarchy is not an insignificant issue, and the true costs of the royal household must be brought to public attention.

Welcome to a discussion about why taxpayers must be able to form their own opinion about the head of state’s use of public funds.

content.title: Resilience in practice – how do we strengthen organisations’ security?
content.description: Technical solutions are not enough to meet today’s security challenges. Real resilience requires technology, skills and organisation to work together. How do we build organisations that can prevent, manage and recover from disruptions and security threats?
content.extendedDescription:
At a time of growing security threats, there is frequent discussion of the need for greater resilience in companies and public authorities. Yet the concept is broad and can mean different things in different organisations. Resilience is not only about technical safeguards, but also about skills, leadership, organisation and the ability to handle unexpected events.

The central societal question is how organisations can build robust structures that keep operations running even when something goes wrong. How can technology, human factors and organisational practices be combined to create an effective security system? What capabilities need to be developed to better prevent, detect and manage security threats? The event takes the form of a moderated discussion exploring different perspectives on resilience and security work.

SäkerhetsArenan is organised by SäkerhetsBranschen, Stöldskyddsföreningen, Brandskyddsföreningen, Tryggare Sverige, Säkerhetsföretagen, Företagsuniversitetet and SOFF.

content.title: Setting the right course for shipping
content.description: Shipping needs better conditions for more Swedish shipping companies to establish themselves and grow, and for more transport by water. How do we create robust, sustainable shipping that strengthens Sweden’s trade, competitiveness and preparedness to maintain essential supplies?
content.extendedDescription: Shipping is central to Sweden’s trade, competitiveness and national preparedness. It carries around 90% of the country’s imports and exports and provides jobs, expertise and logistics solutions that are crucial to growth. Swedish shipping companies are at the forefront of new technology and the climate transition, and the industry still has considerable growth potential. Long-term political decisions, competitive regulations and support from public authorities are needed to help more shipping companies grow, bring more ships under the Swedish flag and enable shipping to contribute effectively to the transport system, defence and preparedness. Better conditions create robust, sustainable and modern shipping that strengthens Sweden’s competitiveness, security and preparedness to maintain essential supplies. During the discussion, representatives of shipping companies and decision-makers explore how we can set shipping on the right course and ensure that it remains a strategic resource for Sweden.
content.subject: Infrastructure/transport

content.title: How are Europe’s monarchies faring?
content.description: Europe’s royal houses are under fire over crime and scandals. Are Europe’s royal houses in the process of abolishing themselves?
content.extendedDescription:
The Norwegian monarchy is on shaky ground. A rape trial involving the so-called bonus prince took place during the spring, and many people have been upset by Crown Princess Mette-Marit’s association with a convicted paedophile. It is also not long since Princess Märtha Louise sold the television rights to her wedding to a shaman. Support for the monarchy has fallen sharply in Norway, and abolition is drawing closer.

In the United Kingdom, the former prince Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has been arrested. The British monarchy is being scrutinised from the ground up, and journalists are trying to establish what other members of the royal family knew.

In Sweden, there was much discussion following the publication of the book Den motvillige monarken.

Welcome to a discussion about how Europe’s monarchies are really faring.

content.title: A Sweden without women pensioners in poverty – how do we reform the pension system?
content.description: Sweden’s pension system has long been criticised by trade unions and the women’s movement. It is time for Sweden to introduce a fairer pension system – but what should it look like?
content.extendedDescription:
Seven out of ten blue-collar workers are worried about their pensions. Most start working at a young age and work hard throughout their lives. Many can barely manage to keep working until retirement age, and once they retire, they can barely live on their pensions. Women in blue-collar jobs who have had low wages combined with involuntary part-time work are hit hardest. It is time for Sweden to introduce a fairer pension system – but what should it look like?

Drawing on Handels’ new pensions report, the pension system will be discussed with political representatives from several parties.

content.title: Together for a clean cleaning industry – how do we stop criminal companies in public procurement?
content.description: The criminal economy costs society billions every year, and labour-intensive industries such as cleaning are particularly vulnerable. Today, many legitimate companies in the industry refrain from bidding for public contracts because they are undercut by shady businesses. How do we stop this trend?
content.extendedDescription: Ekobrottsmyndigheten warns of increasingly sophisticated economic crime in which criminal actors systematically use companies as tools to commit offences. According to a report by Brå, people with links to criminal networks are involved in more than 23 000 companies. Labour-intensive industries such as construction, restaurants and cleaning are particularly vulnerable. This development creates a shadow society in which people are exploited while cleaning our schools, hospitals and public authorities, while legitimate cleaning companies are driven out by shady businesses competing for public contracts. Citizens do not receive the services they are entitled to, and money flows from public funds into the black or grey economy. The cleaning industry’s whistleblowing unit FairPlay Städ has exposed several companies, but sees the people behind them continue operating through new businesses. Politicians call for tougher action against crime, but how do they intend to act when companies are used as tools for crime?
speakerTitles: Group Leader, Committee on the Labour Market
Human Rights Lawyer and National Coordinator against Human Trafficking

content.title: AI, loneliness and falling birth rates – threats of our time?
content.description: Drawing on the latest national survey, we sound a warning about some of the most pressing concerns of our time: falling birth rates, AI’s impact on democracy and, not least, growing loneliness in Sweden.
content.extendedDescription: SOM-institutet at Göteborgs universitet has tracked Swedish social trends for 40 years. In June 2026, we are publishing a new research anthology. Drawing on it, this seminar aims to contribute solid empirical knowledge about public opinion on some of the most pressing perceived threats in Sweden today. One topic is fertility – the fact that fewer children per capita are being born in the country. In a dedicated research project, we are studying why Swedes choose not to have children and the divisions underlying these choices. This relates to the issue of loneliness, its prevalence in Sweden and its impact on our lives and health. The increasing use of AI can also be perceived as threatening in several ways. We have therefore examined the public’s views of the risks of AI development in general, and AI-generated disinformation in relation to democratic elections in particular. You are warmly welcome to listen!

content.title: Is a republic a right-wing cause?

content.title: The visitor economy – Sweden’s most underestimated superpower!
content.description: Sweden faces major challenges: social exclusion, gaps in integration and a need for renewed economic strength. Yet a solution already exists – an industry operating throughout the country and bringing people together every day. The visitor economy is a powerful driver of jobs and integration that must be given greater political attention ahead of the election.
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar is for those who want to stay one step ahead – and help shape Sweden’s future. Business, politics and the industry’s most driven leaders come together to set a new agenda: how to unlock the full potential of the visitor economy.
The visitor economy is not a “nice to have”. It is one of Sweden’s most important drivers of jobs, integration and growth – and it is time it received the political weight it deserves. During the seminar, we highlight concrete reforms that can lower barriers to entrepreneurship, create more jobs – especially for young people – and secure the skills the industry needs.
We present Visita’s agenda ahead of the 2026 election and show how Sweden can increase tourism exports, modernise regulations such as the Alcohol Act, and create long-term, predictable conditions for businesses to grow.
This is more than a seminar. It is an opportunity to influence the direction ahead – for an entire industry and for Sweden’s future.
speakerTitles: Head of Planning, Ministry of Finance

content.title: Is a republic a form of government for our time?
content.description: A republic is based on the principle that the head of state is elected by the people or their representatives, in keeping with democratic ideals of equal treatment and participation in decision-making. Is a republic a modern form of government for our time? How could a Swedish republic be designed?
content.extendedDescription:
Before the breakthrough of democracy just over 100 years ago, there were only a few republics in Europe, but growing political movements for democracy challenged the royal houses. During the 1900s, monarchy then disappeared in most countries.

If we do not strive to develop our democracies, their foundations risk being weakened. We cannot take our political freedoms and rights for granted. If we want to preserve democracy, we must strive for it, develop it and resist every step that weakens it.

Welcome to a discussion about how we can develop democracy in Sweden by abolishing the monarchy!

content.title: Creative bureaucracy for public sector renewal
content.description: The challenges of the future require new ways of thinking, collaborating and making decisions. We address the risk that the everyday practice of democracy is reduced to rigid processes unable to deal with complexity and uncertainty.

The creative bureaucracy festival offers a space for making meaning, reflection and public sector renewal.

At this opening event at Donnerska huset, we replace traditional seminar culture with experiential, facilitated and artistic formats to try new ways of meeting. Through curious conversations between public sector leaders, artists and change leaders, we lay the foundations for a lasting Nordic hub for creative bureaucracy.

Inspired by the Creative Bureaucracy Festival in Berlin, this becomes a place where the public sector reflects on itself, tries new perspectives and develops shared capabilities.

The festival opening on 23 June at 11 at Donnerska huset aims to renew Almedalen through human-centred formats that highlight the public sector’s courage, responsibility and new tools we can use to navigate complexity and uncertainty.

content.title: Inadequate public transport, electrification and petrol station closures – how can rural areas achieve sustainable access?
content.description: Rural areas risk falling behind in the transport transition. Centralised services, withdrawn public transport and petrol station closures affect access, while electrification progresses slowly. How can sustainable access be secured on the basis of rural residents’ needs and circumstances?
content.extendedDescription:
Rural areas face major challenges in the transition to a more sustainable transport system. The public transport industry’s goal of increasing its share of travel risks disadvantaging services in more sparsely populated areas. When services are centralised and public transport is withdrawn, there are often no realistic alternatives to the car. At the same time, rural residents often have lower incomes and older vehicles, delaying the uptake of electric cars. The closure of a local petrol station therefore risks hitting rural residents hard, also because the station often plays an important role as a local meeting place and a hub for services and businesses.
How can we create sustainable access in rural areas based on residents’ needs and circumstances? How can electrification be accelerated even in sparsely populated areas? How do we ensure that petrol stations and other basic services remain for as long as they are needed? And how can municipalities and regions support innovative solutions to strengthen access and vitality in rural areas?

content.title: From healthcare waiting lists to public health – who takes responsibility for the silent common diseases?
content.description: Healthcare is voters’ most important issue ahead of the 2026 election. Meanwhile, one of Swedish healthcare’s least noticed failures continues: time and again, we fail to detect and treat some of our most common diseases early enough.
content.extendedDescription:
In Folkhälsodalen’s major election debate, we shift the focus from waiting lists to the diseases that go undetected – and to what the parties want to do to ensure that more people receive the right diagnosis and treatment in time.

We start with some of our biggest public health challenges:
- High blood pressure

content.title: Brain-friendly environments – a key to Sweden’s competitiveness?
content.description: Sweden’s competitiveness faces a new reality: people’s focus, creativity and mental resilience are a crucial resource in a modern economy. How can business and the public sector shape the built environment to strengthen cognitive ability, productivity and growth?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden’s competitiveness and resilience are now shaped by how well we harness people’s focus, creativity and cognitive stamina. Internationally, this development is described as the emergence of the Brain Economy, in which the brain’s capacity is seen as a crucial strategic asset. In a time marked by information overload, a fast pace and growing complexity – increasingly referred to as “mental pollution” – the way we design our workplaces, schools and cities becomes strategically decisive.

When environments do not support brain function, we risk reduced productivity, increasing ill health and lost capacity for innovation. Neuroarchitecture draws on research into how light, sound, spatial organisation and material choices affect the brain’s work, and thus our ability to perform, think clearly and recover.

The seminar takes the form of a panel discussion bringing together different perspectives on how Sweden can take a leading role in this field.

content.title: Has Gotland found a new path between unemployment and skills shortages?
content.description: Gotland faces challenges from the centralisation of support measures, a declining working-age population and employers struggling to find the skills they need when recruiting. For three years, we have worked actively to match people experiencing social exclusion with businesses on the island and the public sector.
content.extendedDescription: Come and hear how we have involved business in local labour market policy. What happens when companies employ people whom others have written off? In 2023, the Gotland forward project was awarded 20.8 million from Europeiska socialfonden and 1.2 million from Region Gotland to help 280 Gotland residents find a job or start studying. An overarching aim was also to increase understanding between public authorities and business. Political governance sometimes clashes with B2B, but how do we work through that in the best way? Through joint action, local agreements and an IOP (a partnership between civil society and the public sector) with a business organisation, we have successfully put several outcomes into practice. Our engaged panel shares perspectives on what this has meant for their organisations and for Gotland. Learn from Gotland’s example – and take concrete perspectives home to your municipality, region or organisation.

content.title: Can industry and electricity producers reach the energy agreement that politicians cannot?
content.description: How does the energy market cope when politics stands still? Industry’s electricity needs are growing rapidly as electrification progresses, while the expansion of new electricity generation has slowed sharply during the current parliamentary term.
content.extendedDescription:
Analyses indicate that the imbalance between growing electricity demand and the capacity being built risks driving electricity prices sharply higher in several bidding zones within the next few years. Rising electricity costs make it harder for industry to electrify, invest and compete internationally.

In this seminar, we show how developments through to 2035 affect electricity prices, industrial competitiveness and the pace of the climate transition. What is at stake if electricity generation fails to keep pace with demand, and how can the risks be managed when long-term political ground rules are still lacking?

The seminar begins with a presentation of current analysis and forecasts for electricity market developments. This is followed by a panel discussion on the consequences for industry, the energy market and investment, and the choices that are crucial to avoiding higher costs and lost competitiveness.

content.title: Organising movements – how do we build movements that outlive us?
content.description: In recent years, we have seen a growing wave of engagement and mobilisation in response to global injustices and social developments in Sweden. At the same time, questions arise about organising, sustainability and how movements can build lasting change.
content.extendedDescription:
In recent years, we have seen a growing wave of engagement and mobilisation in response to people’s frustration and concern about injustices in Sweden and around the world. New networks and initiatives have emerged, while more people are joining established popular, peace and climate movements.

At the same time, questions arise about sustainability and the long term. How do we build movements that endure? How do we move from mobilisation and actions to organising and lasting political influence? What has worked – and what lessons do we need to take forward? And can different movements be brought together as a common force?

The discussion brings together people with experience of mobilisation, organising and movement-building to explore sustainability, strategies and how to build movements that do not depend on individual people, but can grow, develop and sustain change over time.

The discussion lasts approximately 60 minutes and is followed by time for mingling, networking and sharing experiences for all participants and audience members.

content.title: Ukraine defends the free world now - Will the world be there for Ukraine long term?
content.description: Is rebuilding Ukraine a shared responsibility for Europe and the world? What does rebuild Ukraine mean? Who will be there? At the same time, how can Ukraine, through its experience, expertise, and resilience, contribute to Europe’s future security,  democratic values, and crisis preparedness.
content.extendedDescription:
Meet ambassadors from several countries sharing their perspectives on future partnerships and support for Ukraine. Large parts of Ukraine lie in ruins, and reconstruction may become the largest rebuilding effort in modern history. But rebuilding Ukraine is not only about roads, bridges, and buildings. It is also about restoring democratic institutions, rebuilding communities, and supporting the physical and psychological wellbeing of millions of people affected by war. Who should take responsibility for rebuilding the country – Ukraine itself, Europe, or the wider international community?

This conversation will also explore Ukraine’s potential contribution to Europe and the wider international community. Through its experience of resilience, innovation under extreme pressure, and the rebuilding of critical infrastructure and institutions, Ukraine has knowledge, skills, and perspectives that can strengthen Europe’s long-term security, democratic values, and crisis preparedness.

content.title: Halving VAT on food – at what price, and at whose expense?
content.description: Lower VAT on food can improve public health, but it is both expensive and a blunt instrument. It can enable more people to choose nutritious food. At the same time, however, it lowers the price of both healthy and unhealthy food for all income groups. How can we take the reform further to benefit public health as effectively as possible?
content.extendedDescription:
Lower VAT on food is sometimes presented as a tool for improving public health, but it is both expensive and a blunt instrument. It can indeed reduce financial stress in vulnerable households and make it easier to choose nutritious food, especially for families with children, which may improve health in the longer term. At the same time, it lowers the price of both healthy and unhealthy food, applies equally to all income groups and risks crowding out other, more effective public health measures.
From a public health perspective, the conclusion is therefore that a general reduction in VAT on food has limited influence on people’s actual eating habits. More targeted measures include lower prices for fruit and vegetables, higher taxes on unhealthy products, targeted support for low-income households, and investment in school meals and preventive work.

content.title: Research policy for the humanities – a national necessity?
content.description: Sweden wants to be a knowledge nation equipped for the future. Yet research policy for the humanities is currently both unclear and inadequate. What does responsible research policy for the humanities look like? How do we create the conditions for world-leading humanities research?
content.extendedDescription:
Tackling today’s societal challenges requires solid knowledge and expertise across all fields of research. Yet the latest research bill formulated a research policy that largely left out the humanities. How can Sweden navigate global crises without languages, an understanding of democracy, ethics and religion, and knowledge of history? Can research policy without the humanities really meet society’s challenges?
This year’s report from the think tank Humtank focuses on research policy for the humanities. This seminar presents the report and offers concrete proposals for how Swedish research policy can strengthen both basic and cutting-edge research.
Responsible research policy for the humanities needs to safeguard democracy, security and academic freedom. Strengthening Sweden’s knowledge preparedness can give researchers the opportunity to work together towards such a reality, while giving individual researchers and research groups the conditions to become world leaders in their fields.

content.title: Can Sweden manage without a research policy for the humanities?
content.description: Swedish research policy is currently strongly focused on STEM subjects. At the same time, most people agree that our democratic society requires knowledge from the humanities. How do these positions fit together? What needs to be done to strengthen Swedish humanities research?
content.extendedDescription:
National policy on research and higher education in Sweden is dominated by a focus on the so-called STEM subjects and medical research. Strategies for the humanities have been neglected.
The lack of a research policy for the humanities creates a range of problems. An increasing share of humanities research funding is politically directed rather than researcher-led. Success rates for government research grants have reached rock bottom, and eroded funding for teaching leaves fewer and fewer humanities academics with time for research within their jobs. At the same time, knowledge from the humanities appears indispensable for addressing the crises and challenges of our time.
This seminar draws on the think tank Humtank’s report on research policy for the humanities and discusses key questions for Sweden as a knowledge nation. What measures are needed to develop humanities research? What kinds of humanities research should be supported, and how? What should researchers themselves do, and what requires political action?

content.title: Biogas as part of Sweden’s total defence – a key to a secure energy supply
content.description: The world has entered a period of increased instability. Conflicts in the Middle East and Russia’s continuing war in Ukraine affect energy markets. Sweden needs to strengthen its own resilience. In this situation, biogas plays an important role as a domestic, flexible and storable energy source.
content.extendedDescription: It can be used in transport, industry and critical societal functions, contributing to a robust energy system and stronger total defence. Biogas complements electricity generation and other renewable energy sources by being dispatchable and quickly available during disruptions. It also offers climate benefits, circular resource management and opportunities for regional development through local value chains. But for biogas to scale up at the pace required by the international situation, long-term political conditions are needed. The industry needs support systems that remain stable across parliamentary terms, clear national targets and continued prioritisation of both the green transition and national self-sufficiency. With the right conditions, Sweden can continue investing in production, infrastructure and innovation that strengthen our energy security. This seminar brings together decision-makers, business representatives and experts to discuss the role of biogas in a more resilient energy system.

content.title: Sweden has energy – so how do we use it most intelligently?
content.description: Sweden’s competitiveness depends not on whether we have energy solutions, but on whether we use them intelligently. New ways of working and shared goals can free up power capacity without new infrastructure, making the energy transition a tangible strength for industry, investment and growth.
content.extendedDescription:
The energy transition is crucial to Sweden’s competitiveness, climate action and societal development. A system-smart approach means moving from silos to collaboration: connecting electrification, flexibility, efficiency, energy storage and demand management in practice. When organisations share perspectives and work towards common goals, power capacity can be freed up without new infrastructure, investments can be used more effectively and uncertainty can be reduced – strengthening both the robustness of the energy system and Sweden’s attractiveness and competitiveness.

The seminar takes the form of a moderated panel discussion with a broad range of perspectives and practical experience of new ways of working. The aim is to show how Sweden’s competitiveness can be strengthened when innovation is implemented in a system-smart way as a result of broader dialogue among stakeholders.

content.title: Why is art doing so well?
content.description: Art – the most disadvantaged and bullied area of the budget – is growing rapidly and spreading through society. Why is that? What is it about art that brings out creative thinking in almost everyone? How does art as self-defence and social development work in practice?

And using artistic thinking to develop the organisation really works. The number of Konstfrämjandet districts has grown from 8 to 20 as we have used artistic exploration to establish new Konstfrämjandet organisations around the country. In addition to the districts, we work with member organisations whose number has more than quadrupled(!) With Bildkonst Sverige, we have also succeeded in organising ourselves to secure more than the marginal 1% of the cultural budget for the visual arts. Doing things together and bringing ideas and people together has become Konstfrämjandet’s method of developing art. Free art is driven by curiosity and a thirst for learning. Art is already where the wording of cultural policy aspires to be. Why is art doing so well, and why is that not reflected in the budget? A number of societal actors unpack the issues and look ahead.

content.title: Synergy or conflicting goals at the intersection of development and security policy
content.description: Sweden's security and development policies are becoming increasingly intertwined, but concrete guidelines are lacking. This raises questions about synergies, conflicting goals and how these policy areas should be coordinated to address global challenges and protect Swedish interests.
content.extendedDescription:
The government emphasises that development policy is a central part of foreign policy and should help strengthen Swedish interests. Meanwhile, the national security strategy highlights several areas, including democracy, migration, health and climate, where development assistance plays a significant role. Despite this, there is still no clear direction on how security and development policy should be integrated in practice.

Expertgruppen för biståndsanalys is currently examining the relationship between these policy areas and identifying possible synergies, overlapping goals and risks of conflicting objectives. What has the study shown so far, and what do its findings mean for decision-makers and development assistance practitioners going forward? A discussion of the choices Sweden needs to make to combine effective development cooperation with stronger national and global security.

content.title: AI is changing the rules – leadership in a new technological world order
content.description: AI and advanced technology are opening up entirely new opportunities. At the same time, a growing gap is emerging between what is possible and what is actually achieved. How do we turn potential into real value? And how do we lead an organisation when technology is changing the rules so rapidly and profoundly?
content.extendedDescription:
We are in a technological transition in which AI and advanced technology are opening up entirely new opportunities. At the same time, a growing gap is emerging between what is possible and what most companies actually manage to achieve.
When knowledge and tools become available to everyone, something else becomes decisive: leadership, direction and the ability to turn potential into real value. How do you lead an organisation when technology is changing the rules so rapidly and profoundly?
In this discussion, we explore what AI leadership means in practice and how Swedish companies can strengthen their competitiveness in a new technological reality.

content.title: The pillars of morality and our political choices
content.description: Morality, and the five pillars on which it rests, is one of the deepest drivers of human behaviour. How is morality shaped among Swedes, and how does it influence our political choices?
content.extendedDescription:
In the latest edition of Gemenskapsbarometern, the social psychological theory Moral Foundations Theory was applied to a large Swedish population for the first time. According to the theory, human morality rests on five pillars: care, fairness, loyalty, authority and sanctity.
Different people prioritise these pillars differently, much as some prefer salty flavours and others sweet ones. These differences may help explain why we think differently about politics and society.
The seminar presents new findings on the distribution of moral foundations in Sweden, including individual variations and geographical patterns. We also discuss how these foundations relate to trust, willingness to defend the country and party political preferences.
content.subject: Research

content.title: Restoring the sea – money down the drain?
content.description: Many natural environments are in poor condition, and Sweden and other EU countries must now restore damaged ecosystems on land and at sea. But what do we gain from restoration if we do not also stop the ongoing degradation of the marine environment? And how can an investment in restoration pay off?
content.extendedDescription: Through the global biodiversity framework, the world's countries have agreed not only to halt degradation but to reverse the negative trend in biodiversity. The EU Nature Restoration Regulation is intended as a tool to achieve this goal. But if the marine environment is simultaneously deteriorating due to wider pressures such as eutrophication and overfishing, is restoration worthwhile, and what does this investment deliver? How do different actors justify their investments? A panel of experts and other stakeholders discusses the conditions for restoration, how investments can pay off and how they can also increase public engagement.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Evidence-based policy – knowledge-led governance or political rhetoric?
content.description: Evidence-based policy is often discussed, but scientific findings seem frequently to be sidelined or subordinated to other interests in practice. How is research used in political decisions, and how can knowledge contribute to better-informed and more legitimate governance?
content.extendedDescription:
The role of knowledge in political decision-making has become increasingly central as complex societal challenges demand rigorous analysis and a long-term perspective. At the same time, experience shows that scientific findings do not always have an impact in practice. Terms such as 'evidence-based policy' are used, while decision-making processes are in reality influenced, and perhaps should be influenced, by institutional, political and communication-related factors.

The event examines how scientific knowledge is used in strategic decision-making and governance. The discussion explores which kinds of knowledge have an impact, how actors use research in policy processes, and how decision-making can be designed to give scientific insights an appropriate place without leading to technocratic solutions.

Short presentations are followed by a discussion between researchers, aiming to highlight the opportunities and limitations of using scientific knowledge in future governance.
