content.title: Who safeguards Sweden's communications when everything else fails?
content.description: When lives are at stake, communications must work. Emergency services, public authorities and essential service providers must be able to trust systems to work across technologies and suppliers. Who is responsible, and what political decisions are needed to secure Sweden's critical connectivity in crisis and war?
content.extendedDescription:
We discuss critical communications as a matter of preparedness and governance, not just technology. What responsibility do politicians have for ensuring secure, reliable connectivity in crisis and war? And how can international standards such as 3GPP contribute to interoperability and reduce vulnerabilities?
RISE brings the perspective of independent testing and research environments, where technology can be developed, tested and verified before it is used when it really matters. Together with representatives from politics, public authorities and operational organisations, we focus on how cooperation, standards and testing environments can strengthen Sweden's preparedness, capacity for innovation and international competitiveness.
Who bears ultimate responsibility for critical communications working in a crisis?
What role do national testing environments and international standards play?
What will it take to make secure communications an integral part of Sweden's total defence and civil preparedness?
speakerTitles: Head of Cybersecurity and Secure Communications
Member of Parliament, Parliamentary Group Leader

content.title: What determines life chances in the neighbourhood: the individual, the family or the area?
content.description: The area where you grow up affects your opportunities in life. But is it individual and family characteristics or the area itself that makes the difference?
content.extendedDescription:
Children grow up in areas with different incomes, schools, levels of safety and resources. Differences between these children often persist well into adulthood. But how much is due to the area itself, and how much can be explained by individual and family circumstances? In this seminar, we present current research seeking to distinguish these neighbourhood effects. The seminar also addresses a central question for future welfare and integration policy: should interventions primarily target areas, through measures such as mixed housing and stronger local schools, or individuals and families, through family support and targeted programmes?

Using new data from Gemenskapsbarometern, including measurements of trust at neighbourhood level, researchers and political representatives discuss how an area affects the people who grow up there.

content.title: The return of borders – people, technology and spatial planning in a new era of security policy
content.description: What do borders do to us? Drawing on ongoing research and the current practices of professional 'border workers' such as police officers, customs officials and politicians, how can national borders be maintained and protected, and how does life in border areas work?
content.extendedDescription: Since the Second World War, we have largely taken borders for granted. Within Schengen, we have made borders invisible and dismantled the lines separating states, cultures and languages. But in recent years, borders have returned to centre stage. The pandemic, the war in Ukraine and rising geopolitical tensions have made borders visible in everyday life, politically, practically and emotionally. Here, we focus particularly on the role of technology in border zones, the legal and practical dilemmas emerging from new forms of policing at borders, and how certain places become militarised.

content.title: Sweden is preparing for war – but who will keep the lights on and people warm?
content.description: Sweden is preparing for war, but who will keep people warm? Heating is essential to public resolve, willingness to defend the country, resilience and total defence. What heating preparedness is needed, what goals must be achieved and who should finance the necessary investments?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is investing SEK 50 billion in civil defence, but the role of the energy system in total defence remains unclear. For society to function in crisis and war, keeping the lights on is not enough: people must also be able to stay warm. Heating is fundamental to public resolve and willingness to defend the country, societal functions and resilience, especially in winter. District heating and combined heat and power therefore play a central role in Sweden's preparedness and total defence.
Experience from Ukraine shows that energy infrastructure quickly becomes a target in modern warfare. This also raises questions about establishing facility defence units, physical protection, repair preparedness, backup power, island operation, emergency stockpiles and other measures to strengthen the endurance of the energy system. But what wartime preparedness should society expect from the energy sector? What functional targets are needed to secure heating? And who should fund preparedness: the state, energy companies or both?
speakerTitles: Head of the Energy Preparedness Department
Head of Industry Policy at Energiföretagen

content.title: The cost of caregiving – can you work and parent a child with a neurodevelopmental disability without breaking down?
content.description: Being the parent of a child with a neurodevelopmental disability affects health, social life and, especially, working life. When society does not provide the support the child needs, parents must resolve the often impossible situation of being there for their child while delivering 100% at work. Is that possible?
content.extendedDescription:
For many children with neurodevelopmental disabilities, school is a difficult and sometimes impossible place to be. In the gap between not attending school and compulsory education, parents try to resolve an impossible situation: meeting their child's needs while also performing at work. This greatly affects parents' ability to maintain a functioning working life, and opportunities vary considerably between occupational groups.
Parenthood can mean giving up career progression, reducing working hours or stopping work altogether. Parents also risk their own health, and sick leave is common.

This is a loss for both individuals and society as a whole, for employers and employees alike.

The seminar discusses parents' needs, employers' responsibilities and circumstances, the role of trade unions, and political responsibility for enabling parents of children with neurodevelopmental disabilities to have sustainable working lives and functioning private lives.
speakerTitles: Development Officer for Family Caregiver Support
Author, Parent of a Child with a Neurodevelopmental Disability
Head of the Welfare Policy Unit
Head of Social Services and Gender Equality

content.title: A Cinderella story? Opportunities and challenges in school-age childcare for children with neurodevelopmental disabilities
content.description: School-age childcare is a large and important part of children's school days and also enables parents to work. Yet it is rarely discussed, let alone invested in. Why?
content.extendedDescription:
The challenges at school for pupils with neurodevelopmental disabilities are often discussed, but rarely, if ever, the part of the school day where children spend at least as much time: school-age childcare.

During the seminar, we present our latest report, Orka fritids, which clearly shows how difficult the childcare situation is for pupils with neurodevelopmental disabilities and how challenging staff conditions are for meeting their needs.

We then discuss what is needed for school-age childcare to move from being a service that takes a back seat, fills gaps and constantly solves problems to one that can genuinely be a protective factor for these pupils. A service able to meet, recognise and strengthen these children and truly help each child develop their full potential. What conditions, challenges and opportunities exist, and what must we do to transform school-age childcare from the school's Cinderella into a real protective factor for these children?
content.subject: Education

content.title: The humanities and politics – how can we build better dialogue for the future?
content.description: How can humanities research contribute to political decisions? Today's complex societal challenges require knowledge of culture, language, history and ethics. Yet structures for open dialogue between humanities researchers and politicians are lacking. How can this dialogue be strengthened? What risks and opportunities are there?
content.extendedDescription:
People are at the centre of the major changes, problems and challenges of our time. Whether the issue is security policy, AI, climate or global health, addressing it politically requires an understanding of interpersonal relationships. Humanities research plays a crucial role here. Yet while many humanities researchers feel their findings are rarely sought in political contexts, politicians need concrete and accessible evidence.
In this seminar, we discuss how dialogue and cooperation between humanities researchers and politicians can be strengthened. Do researchers need to communicate their findings differently? Does politics need other ways of gathering knowledge? What risks does dialogue between research and politics involve? And what opportunities arise if the humanities gain a more established place in political decision-making?

content.title: Knowledge preparedness – what value do the humanities offer in an uncertain future?
content.description: Since it is impossible to know what the next societal crisis will be, we need to prepare for the unpredictable. This includes knowledge preparedness. Previous international crises have shown that humanities research is crucial to societal resilience. How can its role in preparedness be strengthened?
content.extendedDescription:
In troubled times, we need to prepare for the future. But crisis plans and material preparedness are not enough. We also need a broad knowledge base across all disciplines to face the unexpected. Robust knowledge preparedness rests on research whose full potential we discover only when it becomes indispensable.
The pandemic made it clear that medical expertise alone was not enough. Crucial questions, such as how vaccine doses should be distributed fairly, were addressed with the help of humanities research. The existential crises we now face have also sparked interest in existential preparedness, to which humanities scholars are particularly well placed to contribute.
Despite this, opportunities for the basic research that strengthens preparedness are limited. How have humanities researchers contributed to Swedish knowledge preparedness so far, and how can they do so in the future? What conditions are needed for Sweden to build a resilient society?
content.subject: Research

content.title: A sense of justice? Swedish public attitudes towards punishment
content.description: For several years, crime and punishment have been priorities for politicians and voters alike. Extensive changes to criminal policy are being implemented, with tougher sentences in several areas expected to increase the prison population. How does the public view this political development?
content.extendedDescription:
Crime and punishment are high on the political agenda, and interest in criminal policy, as well as fear of crime, has increased among Swedish voters. There is strong political interest in meeting public wishes on punishment, and a common premise in the debate is that the public wants tougher sentences than current judicial practice provides.
In a national study, we examine how people in Sweden view punishment in general; what sentences they consider appropriate when presented with specific case descriptions; what they know about current practice; and how different emotions interact with views on punishment.
Maintaining confidence in the justice system requires a balance between the public's sense of justice and the state's judicial practice. Deeper knowledge of people's attitudes and emotions concerning punishment is therefore essential to trust in the rule of law.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: Excellent research – does society need excellent science?
content.description: The Swedish government and the EU are investing heavily in excellent science. Swedish researchers are expected to become the best and lead the race to develop groundbreaking technology. But why is producing exceptional research so important? What is it expected to deliver? And can Sweden really become top of the class?
content.extendedDescription:
The government identifies groundbreaking research as one of the most important ways for Sweden to increase economic productivity. Excellent science is presented as crucial to national development and Sweden's continued ability to compete globally. But who benefits from excellent research? And what happens to humanities research when excellence is equated with interdisciplinarity and directed towards groundbreaking technology?
Previous inquiries have shown that Swedish excellence initiatives have done little to make research globally competitive. Given the enormous resources invested in new technologies such as AI, quantum computers and drones, one may ask whether Swedish research really has the conditions to lead technological development. Questions concerning democratic control of technology, where humanities research is crucial, could offer Sweden another opportunity.
speakerTitles: Professor of Philosophy and Deputy CEO

content.title: An artificial public sphere – humanities perspectives on what AI does to democratic debate
content.description: The smallest unit of democracy is the human being. Democratic citizenship requires public debate. Can democracy survive when the public sphere is dominated by machine learning and optimisation logic? What does an artificial public sphere mean for democracy and human rights?
content.extendedDescription:
What are the consequences of artificial knowledge production for democratic debate? What happens to human rights when human knowledge and experience are treated as training data for statistical models?
Machine learning is now embedded in the systems we use to search for information, read news and take part in debate. It is present in feeds, search engines, recommendation systems and production tools. Machine learning creates knowledge by finding patterns in large volumes of data and optimising probabilities. This is not a neutral process. What is unusual, new or underrepresented is filtered out. What deviates or disrupts risks never becoming a political voice. The result is a public sphere that reproduces the familiar rather than opening up to the unknown.
The seminar discusses where democratic knowledge is created today. What can humanities research tell us about today's artificial public sphere, and conversely, does today's information landscape require a different humanities?
speakerTitles: Professor of Media and Communication Studies

content.title: How healthy is Swedish democracy?
content.description: Public support for democracy, trust in politicians and perceptions of whether democracy is under threat are issues that engage Swedes. Previous reports showed that democracy in Sweden is being questioned, but that the desire for change is strong. How is democracy faring this year?
content.extendedDescription:
Almedalsveckan has developed into an important democratic meeting place where different societal interests meet in respectful dialogue. Political parties, private businesses, public sector organisations and many civil society organisations are represented here. But how healthy is Swedish democracy? For the fifth consecutive year, Demokratirapporten maps current Swedish attitudes towards democracy and provides a factual basis for discussing its state.

Last year's findings included that four in ten Swedes considered democracy under threat. Many voters also questioned politicians' trust in citizens, while a significant proportion expressed scepticism about the news media's agenda. At the same time, a clear majority, 97 per cent, believed democracy was worth defending. But what does this year's picture look like?

content.title: Can music and choral singing address young people's hopelessness and create meaning?
content.description: How can we give more young people hope and meaning? Perhaps the solutions already exist, in our schools and choirs, if we dare to invest in what we know works. Research and practice show how singing contributes to mental health and social cohesion, strengthening self-esteem, community and hope for the future.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar highlights one of the most pressing issues of our time: how can we address young people's hopelessness and sense of meaninglessness? Our starting point is that solutions already exist, right in schools and cultural life. Across Sweden's music sector, music teachers and choir leaders see daily how singing and making music strengthen self-esteem, belonging and hope for the future.
Choral singing is more than an artistic activity. It develops listening, responsibility and cooperation, and creates spaces where every voice counts. In a choir, differences become a strength and community grows organically. Young people experience being genuinely needed and seen within collective meaning-making.
The discussion brings research and practice together to show how music contributes to mental health and social cohesion. We want to highlight bold decisions that strengthen what already works, giving more young people hope and meaning.

content.title: How we can strengthen Sweden's voice in the EU
content.description: The greatest opportunities to influence EU decision-making come early, before a proposal is on the table. While the national level is primarily responsible for negotiating completed proposals, several Swedish actors engage much earlier on a range of issues. How can we cooperate to maximise the benefit for Sweden?
content.extendedDescription:
Europe faces major challenges, and many signs point towards greater centralisation, making it harder to develop place-based solutions and increasing the distance from citizens. How can we achieve effective communication between regional, national and European levels? Today, Sweden's national level seeks input on EU initiatives primarily through consultations, often late in the EU decision-making process, during implementation. This can lead to misunderstandings, increased workloads and costs. Swedish regions have long made their voices heard early in EU decision-making and have built valuable networks that can provide Sweden with important information and opportunities to influence outcomes.
By improving Swedish dialogue on EU initiatives between regional and national levels, we could give Swedish positions greater impact before EU-level decisions are made. Better dialogue would also support effective implementation of EU decisions in Sweden. Let us make use of one another's strengths for a stronger Swedish voice in the EU!

content.title: Resilience in Sweden's municipalities and regions – in war and peace
content.description: A changing world increases Sweden's need for resilience. Military capability and self-sufficiency are often highlighted, but what access to transport, energy and culture can we expect across the country in a crisis? How prepared are we for threats to society's foundation: democracy?
content.extendedDescription:
Growing global tensions have forced the EU to focus more on Europe's competitiveness and security. Much concerns reducing dependencies and increasing self-sufficiency. Yet the war in Ukraine has demonstrated the importance of strong public services during crises. Alongside military functions, people need to heat their homes, reach work and healthcare, and access culture that makes life worth living and builds understanding and resilience.
The EU's changing focus is expected to affect regional work. We know resilience grows from below through place-specific solutions. Is this sufficiently reflected in Sweden's regional development remit?
Societal resilience is central to free and fair elections, which require a democracy that earns citizens' trust and engagement. What internal and external threats face democracy as Sweden goes to the polls this autumn?

content.title: Digital sovereignty for Sweden and Europe
content.description: Chip development, AI and cloud services are new instruments of power — and Europe is dependent. How do we strengthen our digital sovereignty through smarter procurement?
content.extendedDescription:
We live in a time when hardware, software, AI models and cloud services have become strategic instruments of power. Sweden and Europe depend heavily on a handful of global players, creating risks for innovation, security and self-determination. Critical societal functions need to work and must not be something someone else can switch off.
Digital sovereignty is about resilience and long-term capability, not isolation. The choices we make today shape the future, and we can achieve a great deal without waiting for legislation. The purchasing power of European public authorities and businesses is a powerful tool already available to us.
The seminar brings together those making strategic technology decisions in the public sector and business. We highlight concrete examples from organisations that have moved towards European alternatives, discuss what is required of buyers and suppliers, and identify practical policy implications for Sweden and Europe.

content.title: When crisis strikes – who takes responsibility locally in Sweden?
content.description: More and more Swedes believe the country faces a serious crisis in the next few years. Greater demands are being placed on civil society and the financial sector, while almost half of Swedes have made no preparations for a financial crisis.
content.extendedDescription:
Financial crisis preparedness is about more than digital services: it is about knowledge, financial buffers and functioning local infrastructure. How do we ensure people can pay, shop and access their money even when systems are disrupted?

It is Tuesday morning. Card terminals are flashing red. Swish is down. Cash machines are empty. You cannot refuel your car or buy food. What happens in your municipality in the first 48 hours? Who pays for the fuel? How do older people buy their medicine? How does the shop get paid? And who takes responsibility when digital Sweden shuts down?

This seminar brings together representatives of banks, authorities and civil society to discuss how we can strengthen Sweden's resilience together, across the country.
content.subject: Economy
speakerTitles: State Secretary to the Minister for Civil Defence

content.title: Climate, conflict and competitiveness: Europe's energy choices in a new world order
content.description: Lower climate requirements, state aid or open competition on equal terms: all are part of the debate, which also concerns becoming more resilient to geopolitical turbulence and environmental risks. How should Europe approach its future energy supply? And how should Sweden act?
content.extendedDescription:
Recent years have repeatedly shown the dangers of dependence on fossil fuel imports. The worldwide economic and industrial disruption caused by the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz illustrates this clearly.

Meanwhile, the World Economic Forum estimates that four of the ten biggest risks to the global economy over the next ten years will be environment-related. Can Europe's politicians stay the course on climate when short-term competitiveness tops the agenda? Many also agree that Sweden is well placed, but what is the path from potential to actual success?

Join a seminar taking a broad approach and asking the big questions. We begin with the global picture and work our way down to what it means for Sweden and Swedish businesses.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: New paths for neighbourhood development — can we build our way out of segregation?
content.description: Segregation in Sweden persists despite extensive investment. New research shows how neighbourhoods affect life chances and how new construction in disadvantaged areas can change their trajectory.
content.extendedDescription:
Segregation in Sweden is the result of more than a century of housing policy, industrial transformation and migration patterns. In this seminar, we present new research mapping how Swedish segregation developed and which types of urban development have created the most mixed and sustainable neighbourhoods over time.
We also discuss which neighbourhood policies have real potential to improve living conditions in poor districts. Housing policy receives particular attention: can new apartment buildings in disadvantaged areas attract new groups, strengthen local services and benefit existing residents? New Swedish data show that well-designed housing projects can reduce poverty and create opportunities for residents to progress rather than be displaced.
Politics, research and municipal experience come together to discuss which models actually work.
Welcome!

content.title: A housing shortage or a responsibility shortage – what is housing policy's real problem?
content.description: If the problem is not primarily a lack of housing but a system with inadequate responsibilities and incentives, how should housing policy be understood? And who actually bears responsibility for housing policy objectives?
content.extendedDescription:
Parliament's objectives require a well-functioning housing market where supply meets need, but in today's hybrid arrangement of central government, municipalities, the market and stakeholder interests, it is unclear who is expected to deliver what. New research suggests that the insider–outsider structure, weak incentives and unclear institutional roles make it harder to achieve the objectives.
We discuss how responsibility should be allocated in a housing policy that does more than dutifully repeat that we must ‘build our way out of the housing shortage’. What lessons can be drawn from other countries' governance models?

A warm welcome!

content.title: Changes unseen in a hundred years – China, Russia and the new aid landscape
content.description: As Western donors withdraw, they create a vacuum that authoritarian actors quickly fill. Both China and Russia are expanding their presence as global development actors. What roles can and should Sweden and the EU play in a more fragmented development landscape?
content.extendedDescription:
China's global influence is increasing while Western aid actors cut their assistance. Like other aid actors, China is keen to support initiatives aligned with its own priorities and interests. Meanwhile, Russian actors have established themselves as key partners in several African countries through a transactional strategy combining military services, access to natural resources and political support. This model differs clearly from traditional Western aid, which is often linked to democracy, institutional development and long-term societal goals.

Join a discussion about what China's and Russia's global ambitions and influence mean for Western and Swedish aid, and for attitudes and values in recipient countries in areas such as gender equality, sustainable development, democracy and human rights.

content.title: Health as an engine of growth
content.description: Ill health, sickness absence and early departure from working life cause substantial production losses in Sweden. The OECD has estimated that improved health and longer life expectancy explain around half of GDP growth during the twentieth century. Yet health is often treated primarily as a cost.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's future growth increasingly depends on population health. An ageing population, rising chronic disease and high sickness absence put pressure on workforce size and productivity. Meanwhile, knowledge is growing about how prevention, early diagnosis, better treatment and new technologies can strengthen people's ability to work and participate in working life.
Economically, ill health is much more than a healthcare budget issue. Only around a third of its costs arise within the healthcare system itself. Most consist of lost production, reduced labour-force participation, lower productivity and social insurance costs. Improving health therefore has effects far beyond healthcare: more hours worked, higher productivity and longer working lives.
The seminar discusses how health can be understood and managed as a strategic growth factor.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Geographical divides in an election year: how is politics affected?
content.description: Geographical differences have become a growing source of polarisation around the world. Divides between urban and rural areas, but also within cities, affect political views. How is Swedish politics affected when people feel that different places offer entirely different prospects for the future?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is changing, and differences between parts of the country are becoming increasingly apparent. In major and medium-sized cities, both economic and social divides are growing, with segregation, integration and unequal life chances shaping everyday life. Meanwhile, many people in rural and sparsely populated areas feel they are being left behind and that decisions are made far from their reality.

In this seminar, we examine polarisation between places, urban versus rural, and within places, where differences between neighbourhoods are growing in both larger and medium-sized municipalities. We also discuss what research shows about migration patterns: which areas people leave, where they move to and which values and experiences they bring with them.

Drawing on new research, researchers and politicians meet to discuss how geographical divides arise, what drives them and what consequences they have for politics, the election year and the future.

Welcome!

content.title: Health as a strategy, not a perk
content.description: Many employers invest in wellness allowances to reduce the negative health effects of heavy workloads. This is despite scientific studies showing that systematically implemented health processes can have major effects on productivity, work capacity and well-being.
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar highlights how systematic, management-led health processes can create real improvements in health. We address what managers and leadership teams need to know to make health part of their organisation's core strategy. We discuss the fact that dangerously low fitness levels have almost doubled over the past 30 years, contributing to reduced work capacity and increased ill health.

For health programmes to succeed, an organisation's leadership must take overall responsibility and establish an action plan with clear parameters and goals, as part of a healthy organisational culture. Under this plan, unit managers are tasked with being role models and ensuring implementation at unit level. This seminar aims to motivate managers to address health more systematically, generating effective, sustainable improvements throughout the organisation. Drawing on scientific studies and their own experience, participants suggest activities.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Lifelong learning — how do we take responsibility?
content.description: As the labour market changes rapidly through technological development, AI and new skills requirements, lifelong learning becomes crucial. But who is responsible for the transition — central government, regions, employers or individuals?
content.extendedDescription:
The labour market is changing ever faster. Digitalisation, AI and technological development affect both tasks and skills requirements in many professions.
This makes lifelong learning a central issue for individuals, employers and society. Yet the division of responsibility is often unclear. Who should be responsible for enabling people to adapt throughout a long working life?
Should responsibility lie primarily with individuals themselves, employers or society's education system? And how can different organisations cooperate to create effective routes to transition?
The discussion particularly highlights the role of folk high schools and other education providers, opportunities to validate existing skills and the risk of groups being left behind as the labour market changes rapidly. The seminar considers what an effective system for lifelong learning might look like in a time of rapid transition.

content.title: Precision prevention for better health – are postcodes more important than genes?
content.description: Sweden's population is ageing, and we need to stay healthy for longer if health and social care are not to collapse. Yet health foundations are laid during childhood. Could precision prevention bring a breakthrough in more effective health promotion and disease prevention?
content.extendedDescription:
WHO says that 80% of cardiovascular disease and 40% of cancer can be prevented. Meanwhile, several risk factors are increasing in a rapidly ageing population. Healthcare spends 3% of its budget on promotion and prevention, and VAT was cut on all food on 1 April, despite evidence that a shift in food taxation could save 700 lives a year. Municipalities have no health department, yet shape the most important determinants of health.

content.title: How are civilians affected by persistently high levels of conflict worldwide?
content.description: Violence worldwide has increased dramatically in recent years. Many civilians die directly from violence in conflict zones, but many more suffer indirect effects. What does research say about conflict's consequences for civilians? What is the situation in Ukraine?
content.extendedDescription:
The UCDP conflict data programme at Uppsala universitet presents the global situation and discusses the effects of high conflict levels on civilians. UCDP data shows that violence worldwide has indeed increased dramatically in recent years. Our media are filled with reports of wars and threats of war. In Sweden, Russia's war against Ukraine and the war between Israel and Hamas have received particular attention. Other extremely bloody conflicts have occurred or continue in countries including Ethiopia, Sudan and Mexico without receiving the same attention.

Many civilians die directly from violence in conflict zones, but many more suffer indirect effects. The best available estimates suggest that 10–20 times as many people die from wars' indirect effects. This panel examines research on conflict's consequences for civilians in affected areas and discusses the situation on the ground in Ukraine.

content.title: Obliged to say yes, required to say no – the right to a bank account versus anti-money laundering
content.description: More people risk being excluded from the financial system because of the conflict between the obligation to enter into contracts and anti-money laundering legislation. This is not only a problem for individuals – it is a societal problem.
content.extendedDescription:
Earlier this year, the government tasked Finansinspektionen with making it easier for banks to meet their obligations to provide basic banking services. The assignment highlights an issue that has become increasingly pressing as requirements for banks' anti-money laundering work have tightened.

Banks in Sweden often find themselves at the intersection of two regulatory frameworks that can pull in different directions: the Payment Services Act's requirements for access to basic banking services and the Anti-Money Laundering Act's requirements for customer due diligence and risk management. How should these interests be balanced? Where is the boundary between necessary risk management and financial exclusion? And what guidance do banks need to make legally sound and proportionate decisions?

As more people risk being excluded from the financial system, the issue becomes bigger than a matter of legal interpretation. It concerns trust, inclusion and the ability to participate fully in society.

content.title: How are AI, personalisation and a changing working life reshaping future pensions?
content.description: New technology and better use of data offer opportunities to make pensions more accessible, understandable and tailored to individuals. Meanwhile, labour market developments raise questions about responsibility, trust in the system and employers' role in people's long-term security.
content.extendedDescription: Working life is changing: people change jobs more often, combine work and retirement, take breaks and work longer than previous generations. Meanwhile, AI and better access to data enable an entirely new kind of transparency and pension planning: personal, proactive and accessible to all. But progress does not happen automatically. This conversation explores what is actually required of technology, regulation and employers who want to take responsibility for their employees' long-term security.
content.subject: Employment/labour market

content.title: Sweden is transitioning – what would sustainability experts propose if they were in government?
content.description: Sweden has ambitious climate targets and wants to become one of the world's first fossil-free welfare nations. Proposals for the necessary measures are now being presented.
content.extendedDescription:
Ahead of the 2026 election, Aktuell Hållbarhet launches Solskensregeringen, tasked with identifying the measures Sweden needs for the transition. Seven ‘ministers’, all leading experts in their fields, present proposals for making Sweden more sustainable. Topics include green jobs that counter exclusion, tax shifts, cities and nature's role, infrastructure and energy sovereignty.
Markus Wråke – Minister for Energy

content.title: Diplomacy and the nuclear threat
content.description: The world is entering a new phase of nuclear rearmament. What are the prospects for diplomatic efforts to reduce the nuclear threat after the war in Iran and the expiry of the last bilateral nuclear arms agreement between Russia and the USA? What does the future hold for the Non-Proliferation Treaty?
content.extendedDescription:
Join a panel discussion with experts in nuclear arms control agreements, diplomacy and multilateral negotiations. The panel comments on the current situation and discusses the diplomatic challenges ahead. The seminar will address the following questions:

• What are the prospects for diplomacy after a dramatic spring – the war in Iran, the expired New START Treaty and the conclusion of the Non-Proliferation Treaty Review Conference?
• What makes nuclear disarmament so difficult?
• How does growing great-power rivalry affect ongoing diplomacy in this field?
• How should small and medium-sized states without nuclear weapons act? What can Sweden do?
